strengths: The paper addresses a relevant, practical NLP evaluation problem: how collaboration settings influence the outputs of interactive qualitative coding systems.
Comparing three distinct approaches across two contrasting corpora provides useful empirical breadth. Holding initial partitions fixed within systems removes one source of variation.

The manual audit of 2,400 document–theme pairs provides valuable evidence beyond embedding-based proxies. Two annotators evaluate each assignment, disagreements are adjudicated, and agreement is reported transparently (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632 and 0.696).

The presentation clearly separates consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness. Operational descriptions, prompt templates, final theme lists, and a stated public code/data release support inspection and reuse.
weaknesses: The experimental contrast does not isolate collaboration modality as claimed. Asynchronous outputs are individual codebooks without consolidation, whereas synchronous outputs come from three-person groups. This supports a narrower individual-versus-group comparison. Reused participants always perform asynchronous coding first, introducing possible practice effects, and comparable time or effort budgets are not reported. The acknowledged omission of consolidation materially limits conclusions about asynchronous collaborative workflows.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified. Each system–dataset setting contains only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report numerous unpaired t-tests without identifying the sampling unit or explaining dependencies among themes, document similarities, and reused participants. Treating these lower-level observations as independent would produce pseudoreplication. Analysis respecting the experimental units, confidence intervals, and an explanation of multiple-comparison handling are needed to substantiate the significance claims.

Participant accounting is internally inconsistent. Twelve synchronous sessions with three coders require 36 distinct participants under the stated restriction of at most one synchronous experiment per person, but Section 4.2 reports 33 participants overall. Additionally, the five Climate codebooks have identical theme sets across the relational and LLM approaches (Tables 15–16). A participant-by-session allocation and explicit account of any codebook reuse are necessary to reconstruct the design and its dependencies.

Correctness is not sufficiently defined for reproduction. Figure 4 reports F1, while Section 5.3 describes judgments on sampled document–theme assignments without specifying the ground-truth construction, precision/recall calculation, or averaging procedure. Sampling weights and treatment of unassigned documents are also unclear, and the figure lacks uncertainty estimates. These omissions limit interpretation of an otherwise valuable human audit.

The proposed quality framework needs stronger construct validation. Best-match consistency permits many-to-one alignments, codebooks vary substantially in theme count, and centroid similarities approach 0.98 even when document overlap is low. Sensitivity to theme granularity and embedding choice is not established. Assignment correctness alone does not validate the interpretation that greater embedding cohesiveness indicates deeper or more useful qualitative analysis.

Several explanations exceed the evidence: two corpora differing simultaneously in size, domain, length, and semantic structure cannot isolate effects of complexity or cognitive load, and one implementation per category cannot establish that intervention richness explains collaboration benefits. These should remain hypotheses. The design, inference, and reporting concerns require important revisions before the paper meets the Findings soundness and reproducibility threshold.
